title: Police pepper spray not cause of death of mentally ill man
article: The medical examiner's office has ruled police pepper-spray did not cause the death of a mentally ill man.
Kasim Cakmak, 37, died May 11 from "excited delirium due to chronic paranoid schizophrenia," says a recent report by Chief Medical Examiner Dr. Graeme Dowling.
Cakmak, a diagnosed schizophrenic on medication, was at the Alberta Mental Health Board's downtown Community Living Program when he flew into a rage.
The Mental Health Crisis Response team was called to take him to Alberta Hospital, but he became more upset and slapped a nurse.
Two police officers arrived to assist the transfer and Cakmak got more angry. The officers pepper-sprayed him andhandcuffed him on the ground.
They then noticed he had stopped breathing.

In some rare cases, psychiatric patients and people high on cocaine develop excited delirium. They become quite aggressive and violent, sometimes developing superhuman strength, for no apparent reason, Dowling said.
"When people do restrain them, all of a sudden they stop breathing," Dowling said. "It has nothing to do with the restraint."
A Calgary man with schizophrenia died from excited delirium in 1996, after police pepper-sprayed him during an arrest.
Edmonton police earlier ruled no excessive force was used in Cakmak's case.
The police department and Cakmak's family have both called on the mental-health board to change procedures.
Police said they would have handled things differently had they been warned Cakmak was paranoid and couldn't understand their verbal instructions.
Cakmak, who immigrated from Turkey in 1990, didn't speak English well. His family said they would have gladly come to the clinic to calm him down.
A board spokesperson said a standard procedural review was called after the incident but no comment will be made until a fatality inquiry is held. No date has yet been set.
